Extractive question answering systems can be enhanced with the aid of pre-trained models, but they can be lacking in specialized knowledge for particular languages, such as Romanian. To rectify this, we have developed a model incorporating external knowledge and tailored to the English language, and applied it to the Romanian language through a cross-lingual transfer method. This method was then employed to create a complex Romanian knowledge base for question answering, utilizing a unique hybrid approach that combines knowledge and simple text-based responses. To evaluate the effectiveness of our system, we have utilized two distinct datasets, one comprising questions from the Open World Tree, and the other comprising questions generated by users from the Wikipedia platform. Our findings reveal that the system we have developed excels in providing accurate answers to user-generated questions on the Wikipedia platform, but struggles with questions from the Open World Tree dataset.

The distribution of missing baryons in the universe is closely tied to the cosmic web's structure, with its smooth gas component filling the gaps between galaxies and galaxy clusters. A new study proposes a method to map the distribution of these missing baryons in the nearby universe by analyzing the diffuse X-ray emissions. The research combines data from the Chandra and XMM-Newton observatories to create a detailed map of the X-ray emissions, which is then used to reconstruct the distribution of missing baryons. The results reveal that the X-ray emissions follow the same patterns as the distribution of galaxies and that the estimated mass of missing baryons in the nearby universe is consistent with previous estimates. The study also suggests that the diffuse X-ray emissions are largely produced by hot gas originating from galaxies.

We propose a novel algorithm for approximating treewidth, with a time efficiency that scales as $k^{O(\log k)}$ for treewidth parameters $k$ of at least 2. This improvement surpasses the previous best algorithm of Grossman et al. and is achieved through a method that combines Courcelle's theorem with a modified version of the Dreyer et al. algorithm. Notably, our approach also accommodates integer treewidth parameters and is adaptable to directed graphs, with a time efficiency that scales as $k^{O(\log k)}$ for directed graphs with a treewidth parameter of at least 2.

Recent research has suggested that Tidal Disruption Events (TDEs) could be a source of Type Ia supernovae mimics, but a direct link between the two phenomena has yet to be confirmed. We have conducted a study of 13 galaxies that experienced a TDE in the past, using the Hubble Space Telescope to analyze their nuclear morphology and the Pan-STARRS catalog to search for young stars associated with the TDE. We have also compared the TDE host galaxies to the host galaxies of SNe Ia, and found that the TDE hosts are more similar to post-starburst galaxies than TDE hosts. We have also discovered that the TDE hosts have lower star-formation rates and mass, and are older than TDE hosts. We have also found that the TDE hosts have higher black hole masses than TDE hosts. We have also used the TDE hosts to constrain the rate of TDEs in the local universe, and found that the TDE rate is lower than previously estimated. We have also found that the TDE rate is lower than the rate of SNe Ia.

This study examines the practical application of reinforcement learning (RL) in 5G radio access networks (5G-RAN). A novel learning-based scheduler called actor-critic learning-based scheduler (ACLS) is proposed to optimize resource block allocation for uplink users by utilizing a deep reinforcement learning framework. The ACLS is trained using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm and relies on a customized reward system that takes into account both user utility and network resource usage. To evaluate ACLS, extensive simulations are conducted within the Open5GS 5G-RAN simulator, comparing its performance to established approaches such as round robin and largest weight (LW) algorithms. The results demonstrate that ACLS outperforms the LW algorithm by 1.6% in terms of user utility and also surpasses the round robin algorithm by 0.8% in terms of user utility.

In recent years, word-level quality estimation has gained significant attention, 
despite initial research focusing primarily on sentence-level quality estimation. 
Building on this foundation, our study explores the potential of word-level 
quality estimation as a component of a pipeline for sentence-level quality 
evaluation. We discovered that a refined word-level quality estimation model can 
serve as a filtering mechanism that filters out low-quality words from input text. 
This, in turn, enables the development of a quality estimation model pipeline 
with enhanced performance, which our experiments on the JRC 2011 corpus demonstrated 
to outperform the baseline model by 1.2 F1 points.

Researchers have introduced a new class of Kerr-de Sitter black holes. The new shadow of this black hole has been analyzed and compared to the standard Kerr-de Sitter shadow. The study found that the shadow of this black hole has distinct differences when considering different parameters, such as the rotation parameter and observer distance. The shadow observed at infinity by an infinity observer was found to be unique to the new black hole, whereas other observers see a shadow similar to Kerr-de Sitter. The study also explored the effect of the new black hole on photon capture and found that the equatorial plane plays a crucial role in this process. The findings of this study are expected to provide valuable insights for future telescopic observations.

A novel, flux-conservative formulation of relativistic hydrodynamics has been developed using the finite-volumes methods, ensuring its numerical implementations preserve the physical properties of conserved variables and adhere to the relativistic laws under any discretization scheme. This new formulation, built on the exact two-speed wave front, ensures the exact satisfaction of the relativistic conservation laws within the finite-volumes grid, without relying on approximate operators as in previous methods. Notably, the new formulation shares similarities with the well-established finite-volumes methods in non-relativistic plasma and fluid dynamics. To validate its effectiveness, the new method has been compared to other existing methods in a series of numerical tests, including one-dimensional shock-tube problems, two-dimensional Riemann problems, three-dimensional shock-cylinder interactions, and high-energy astrophysical problems such as supernova explosions in various environments. Results show that the new method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, producing results in excellent agreement with experimental data across a wide range of parameters and scenarios.

The $D_{sJ}^-(2520, 2580)$ states are a group of charmed-strange baryons that are being studied using $D^0 K^0_{\rm S}$. Researchers have analyzed a dataset from the BESIII detector, which was obtained through high-energy collisions. They have discovered several $D^0 K^0_{\rm S}$ resonant structures that are consistent with the $D_{sJ}^-(2063)$, $D_{sJ}^-(2860)$, and $D_{sJ}^-(2739)$ states. The results also show that the $D_{sJ}^-(2573)$ state can decay into $D^{*+} K^0_{\rm S}$. This is the first time that this particular decay has been observed, and the results are consistent with the hypothesis that the $D_{sJ}^-(2573)$ state is a $J^{P} = 0^{+}$ tetraquark. The results from the analysis are consistent with the existing knowledge about the $D_{sJ}^-$ states.

We propose a novel estimation method for the fractal dimensions of functions defined on the Sierpi\'nski Gasket, grounded in the Donsker theorem and multiscale entropy (MSE) analysis. By demonstrating the equivalence between the Sierpi\'nski Gasket and a specific network structure, we establish a link between the two fields of fractals and time series. Our approach is validated through the analysis of a specific example function, the identity function, which exhibits distinct properties at different resolution scales.

To effectively evaluate image understanding models, it's crucial to have high-quality reference questions. However, manually generating such questions is a time-consuming and difficult task. Our research investigates the role of a model-based question generation approach to automatically creating reference questions for images. We introduce a method to guide the question generation model by providing image descriptions as context and employing a similarity metric to influence the question generation process. Our experiments on the Open Images Dataset demonstrate that this guided approach yields more grammatically coherent and relevant questions compared to a baseline model. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the generated questions and propose future research directions.

The Cuspy Matter Power Spectrum (CMPS) model, initially designed to predict the behavior of dark matter halos surrounding dwarf galaxies, has been expanded to include the effects of baryonic matter on the halo structure. By analyzing the impact of various parameters, such as the size and density of the dark matter core, on the CMPS model, a new parameter was introduced to account for the influence of baryonic matter on the halo. This parameter, denoted as delta, was found to be correlated with other parameters, allowing researchers to determine its value based on the mass and redshift of the halo. By comparing the expanded CMPS model with the results from N-body simulations, a good agreement was found, as the model accurately reproduced the effects of baryons on the halo structure. The model was also found to be in agreement with the observed trends in the halo structure, as reported in recent studies.

In SAT solving and theory reasoning, eliminating variables is a widely used technique. However, in the context of quantifier-excluded formulas, this method is problematic. A recent study by the authors has shown that eliminating a single variable from a formula under certain assumptions can be efficiently reduced to a simpler problem involving a single literal. This result was achieved by first converting the formula to a specific type known as CNF-DNF, and then applying a refinement to eliminate pure literals in polynomial time. This technique, known as quasipure literal elimination, has been proven to be correct and can be used to derive a variety of results in the context of quantifier elimination. Interestingly, the authors' technique is more effective in the context of CNF-DNF than a previously known method for pure literal elimination, and it can even handle cases where pure literal elimination is not applicable. A related result has been obtained regarding the application of certain simplification rules in the context of quantifier elimination.

We investigate a $q$-player, $q$-strategy game of unbounded length, allowing for the possibility of a finite number of rounds. Our findings demonstrate that this game can be condensed into a finite game of $q^q$ stages or less, which enables the application of the Folk Theorem to establish the reachability of any Nash equilibrium. Additionally, we show that this game can be converted into a single-stage game, thus enabling the implementation of any Nash equilibrium in the original game.

This study introduces a novel statistical method for multivariate regression trees, enabling the estimation of multiple target variables at various points within the tree through a sequence of independent Gaussian distributions. The method is grounded in the principle of optimal coding and is quantified using the Kullback-Leibler divergence metric. The approach is applied to a multivariate regression task, yielding a statistical model that can be tested using traditional methods such as the likelihood ratio test. The model is further validated through a series of simulations, showing its ability to outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy. The study also explores the model's potential in classification tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in classifying target variables.

This study presents a novel communication-saving approach called Communication-Censored (ComCensored) for distributed algorithmic charging of Electric Vehicles (EVs) in a distributed manner. ComCensored enables efficient communication among distributed algorithmic chargers to minimize communication overhead. By implementing a data-driven strategy, ComCensored decides whether to exchange data or not, thereby significantly reducing the overall communication burden. To validate the ComCensored strategy, we conducted an analysis of its convergence properties and demonstrated its effectiveness through simulations, which showed that ComCensored achieves a 90% reduction in communication overhead compared to traditional methods without compromising charging efficiency.

Accurate estimation of electronic properties is crucial in materials research, 
but it heavily relies on the chosen density functional, which can be time-consuming 
to evaluate, especially for complex structures. To address this issue, we developed 
a linear model that predicts electronic properties using a dataset of density 
matrix values. By incorporating various types of features and selecting the best 
combination, we achieve significant improvements in accuracy when compared to 
traditional methods. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective in 
predicting a range of properties, including band gaps, densities, and chemical 
potentials, for various systems and density functionals, showcasing its versatility 
across different levels of accuracy and a wide range of materials.

The metabolic niche space that a species can occupy is limited by its ability to utilize various energy sources and withstand different environmental conditions, yet the relationship between this space and other species within the same ecosystem is unclear. To address this question, we examined the metabolic niche space of 13 species of bacteria that live in wetlands and their interactions with other species when introduced to different habitats and host environments. Our analysis revealed that the metabolic niche space is influenced by the species' ability to coexist with other species and that larger spaces in the metabolic niche are associated with reduced competition. Notably, we found that the metabolic niche space that a species can occupy is similar across different habitats and host environments, suggesting a link between the species' metabolic capabilities and its ability to thrive in various ecosystems.

The growing implementation of the Internet of Things (IoT) in building management has led to an exponential increase in data generated from sensors, posing a challenge in effectively utilizing this data. To address this, various data processing methods have been explored, but many are resource-intensive or struggle to handle large datasets. To address these limitations, a new approach utilizing the Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAA) technique is proposed, which enables efficient and scalable data processing. By evaluating the SAA method against existing techniques, our results demonstrate that it not only outperforms other methods but is also highly scalable. To further showcase its benefits, a prototype system is presented that leverages SAA to process and analyze large-scale building data, with promising results indicating that it can significantly reduce processing times while maintaining data accuracy.

The origin of hydrogen-poor Type Ic supernovae (SNe Ic) is still a mystery. One theory is that these explosions occur when a massive star merges with a companion star that's already in its final stages. This merger could trigger a series of stellar events, ultimately resulting in the explosion. We've discovered a system that could serve as a prime example of this process. The binary system consists of a star that's emitting light from its surface (the donor) and a companion star that's already in its final stages (the companion). The binary system is located about 2.7 million light-years away and is about 4.5 times the diameter of the solar system. The companion star is about to undergo a supernova, and its explosion is expected to occur within the next 400 years. The binary system is already experiencing a strong gravitational pull due to the stars' close proximity, which is about 0.5 astronomical units. This is a key factor that could trigger a series of stellar events, including a mass transfer from the donor to the companion star. This transfer could eventually lead to the explosion of the donor star, resulting in a hydrogen-poor SN Ic. This binary system is a prime candidate for producing a hydrogen-poor SN Ic, and it may even be observable in the near future.

The classical model of magnetic behavior in two-dimensional materials predicts significant changes in magnetic direction when the strength of magnetic force is very high. This results in highly stable magnetic states that don't allow for any movement. However, at high temperatures, this stability is broken and the magnetic states become randomly distributed. Our research shows that in a magnetic field, this randomness causes the magnetic states to switch direction in a non-linear fashion. This non-linear effect is observed to be influenced by the temperature and the strength of magnetic field. This study provides new insights into the magnetic properties of two-dimensional materials and offers a way to experimentally test the stability of magnetic states in these materials.

In the area of syntax, constituency grammar induction is a key problem. We address this problem through a novel approach that incorporates visual aspects. A trained model, utilizing a transformer architecture, combines the analysis of sentences with images, yielding better performance than previous methods. The effectiveness of our model is demonstrated on both visual and text-only datasets. Moreover, the model provides valuable visual features that aid in understanding the underlying grammatical structure of the language.

A fundamental issue in explainable machine learning is measuring the contribution of model features to specific predictions. Various attribution methods have been developed to address this challenge, but evaluating their performance is complicated due to a lack of standard datasets and criteria for success. To address this issue, we created a collection of 14 datasets and 11 evaluation metrics, and applied 9 attribution methods to them. Our analysis reveals that attribution methods often perform poorly when tested on different datasets, and even when they perform well on a particular dataset, their results are not always reliable. Furthermore, we found that using multiple datasets for evaluation is crucial for accurately assessing attribution methods, and we provide a framework for doing so. Our study's results and datasets are available online.

We investigate a class of traversable wormholes known as generalized Gopakumar-Rupadhyaya spacetimes, which have two distinct shadow images. By using the method of imaging the wormhole by an external massive body, we establish the parameters of the spacetime at the same time. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the secondary shadow is observable in certain conditions and may provide additional information about the wormhole. Additionally, our results indicate that the secondary shadow is more pronounced in generalized Gopakumar-Rupadhyaya spacetimes than in other four-dimensional spherically symmetric black hole spacetimes.

We introduce a novel additive estimate for permutations and leverage this discovery to establish a subadditive estimate for the permanent, with particular implications for matrices with nonnegative entries. This enhanced estimate surpasses the previous subadditivity estimate derived by Linial and Winsor, with the distinction of being valid for all nonnegative matrices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our estimated value lies within a factor of $\log\log N$ of the optimal permanent value for $N\times N$ matrices with nonnegative entries.

This paper explores a class of trimmer models on the triangular lattice that are closely related to the dimer model. It is demonstrated that the dimer model can be reconfigured into a family of trimmer models with adjustable interaction parameters, which retains the symmetry of the triangular lattice. A comprehensive analysis of the trimmer models is conducted, and their phase diagrams are mapped. Notably, the study reveals that the trimmer models display the same critical behavior as the dimer model in certain regions. It is further observed that the trimper models exhibit distinct phases, including an ordered phase, a disordered phase, and a critical phase, which can coexist simultaneously.

This study introduces a novel approach to handle the target unknown issue in
Gaussian Process (GP) models. Initially, we establish a prior distribution
across the feature space, which is then updated with a specific type of
Bayesian evidence to generate a posterior distribution. By integrating a
GP model with an alternative, non-Gaussian prior, we resolve the target
unknown challenge. Our proposed framework is capable of distinguishing between
samples associated with the known target and those with an unknown target
through the derived marginal probability. Our theoretical findings confirm that
the developed method can effectively differentiate between known and unknown
target samples in the feature space. Our experimental results demonstrate the
practical efficacy of this approach.

This research introduces a novel 3D vehicle reconstruction method that leverages a multi-branched Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to achieve vehicle shape normalization. By utilizing a single image, our approach normalizes 3D vehicle meshes to standard sizes, enabling accurate shape analysis without requiring any manual vehicle measurements. The outcome of this normalization process is a refined 3D vehicle shape. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted experiments using a dataset of real-world 3D vehicle meshes and a comparative study with a baseline method that relied on manual vehicle measurements. Our results demonstrate that our method successfully enhances 3D vehicle shape regularization and outperforms the baseline in terms of accuracy.

This research introduces a pioneering method for automatically generating query graphs of a subject graph based on a given natural language question. The proposed method involves a dual-process approach, where a query graph is constructed by initially selecting a starting node, followed by a subsequent and iterative process of node and edge additions guided by semantic reasoning and graph connectivity. The query graph construction method is designed to be flexible, accommodating various query graph sizes and structures. The experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics, while also enhancing the interpretability of the query graph construction process. The associated code and datasets can be accessed via the link provided.

This paper expands on existing research by generalizing the work on linear and linearizable cryptosystems using algebraic methods to infinite alphabets. We build upon a previous study to explore how infinite alphabets impact the types of cryptosystems that can be developed. We establish that any linear cryptosystem defined over an infinite field can be considered equivalent to a previously identified class of cryptosystems, and we also show that an infinite alphabet does not affect the ability of a system to be linearizable. We provide a specific example of a linear cryptosystem that cannot be linearized, even when working with an infinite field, and discuss the potential security implications of this finding.

To identify and disambiguate named entities in large knowledge graphs, we developed a new method that leverages the connections between entities linked to similar images. This approach is based on the assumption that real-world images can provide a more accurate representation of visual relationships between entities than artificially created descriptions. The technique is applied to two distinct disambiguation tasks, one focusing on general entities and the other targeting locations, and is combined with a traditional disambiguation model to improve its performance. The proposed method is applied to two datasets, Google Images and Commonitads, and demonstrates its effectiveness in resolving ambiguities and reducing entity frequency fluctuations.

The authors of this study have determined the electroweak gauge boson self-energy corrections through S, T, and U parameters, and have compared their one-loop results with a corresponding two-loop matched evaluation from the literature. They have also examined the dependence of their results on the electroweak input parameters and the top quark mass. Furthermore, they have calculated the same corrections through a four-loop matching, and have presented their findings in terms of the O(α^4) logarithmic corrections.

In a conventional setup for dynamic view synthesis, we have access to a large dataset of camera poses and corresponding images. However, in this work, we aim to learn a dynamic representation using a single input video. To achieve this, we introduce a novel regularization loss that is based on the inherent characteristics of implicit functions. This characteristic dictates that close points should have similar representations in 3D space. By utilizing this property, we can use the input video to provide a 3D alignment constraint for training. This is achieved by minimizing the Euclidean distance between pixels from different views that are close in 3D space. We also propose a method to learn camera poses that are not available. This involves predicting the camera pose for each frame in the input video and using them to synthesize frames in between. Furthermore, we introduce a technique to learn a pose warping function that allows us to generate new camera poses for unseen frames. Our approach is evaluated on the DTaSet dataset and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of visual quality and plausibility.

This study examines the differential equation $dy = V(y) \, dX^1(t)$, where $V: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is a Borel function and the driving process $X$ is a branched rough path with regularity $\alpha \in (0, \, \frac{1}{3}]$. The research demonstrates that the equation's solution $y$ has a branching rough path solution under specific conditions on the function $V$ and the driving process $X$. The study further explores the relationship between the regularity of the solution's branching path and the regularity of the driving process $X$, establishing that the solution's branchings decay at a rate of $t^{-\alpha/2}$ as $t$ approaches infinity. The study also considers the case of a deterministic function $V$ and shows that the solution's branchings decay at a rate of $t^{-\alpha/2}$, with the solution itself being a branched rough path.

This research explores the application of classical probability measures based on random grain models, specifically Hermite distribution, to derive expressions for non-linear functions using random variable combinations. The study utilizes Charlier polynomials and a simplified form of Mehler's formula to express these functions. Specifically, the work focuses on the density of sums of squares of random variables and a generalised form of this function. The findings are further extended to express non-linear transformations of random variables in terms of L-derivatives and a Laguerre function expansion method.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) have the potential to revolutionize wireless communications by providing an alternative to traditional base stations. RIS technology has gained significant interest due to its low energy consumption, small physical footprint, and ability to be reconfigurable. However, several challenges must be addressed to make RIS-assisted networks a reality, including the development of a control strategy for the RIS elements, the impact of hardware limitations, and the need for efficient transmission methods. This paper provides an overview of RIS technology and discusses the key issues that must be addressed in order to achieve the full potential of RIS-assisted networks. We also introduce a novel approach to designing RIS-assisted communication systems that takes into account the limitations of RIS element phase shifters, leading to more efficient and robust transmission systems. Our proposed method is demonstrated through a detailed analysis of a wireless communication system, where the results show a significant improvement in channel estimation accuracy and the convergence of the RIS-assisted communication protocol.

We introduce a novel method to simplify complex stochastic chemical kinetics by transforming them into continuous-time Markov chains with reduced dimensions. Unlike existing methods, our approach allows the number of dimensions to be controlled by a parameter that can be optimized. The method is based on a mathematical approximation that maintains accuracy under certain conditions and can be adjusted to match the kinetics of the original model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by successfully replicating the dynamics of a specific model and reducing its complexity from 26 to 5 dimensions. The resulting simplified model enables efficient simulations and estimates of various quantities of interest.

Most existing low-bit quantization methods use a single phase of training to develop the low-bit quantized model, which often leads to performance loss compared to full-precision models. To address this issue, we introduce a novel two-phase method called cyclic training, which first trains a 32-bit model and then refines it into a low-bit model. During the first phase, we utilize an innovative loss function to enhance the model's representation of input data. In the second phase, we employ a unique gradient scaling technique to optimize the low-bit model, which is achieved by adjusting the weights' updates through scaling. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated on various datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, where it outperforms state-of-the-art techniques by 0.8% to 1.4% on CIFAR-10 and 1.0% to 2.4% on ImageNet.

Our research indicates that the rate of white dwarf mergers producing Type Ia supernovae is significantly lower than that of the single degenerate channel, with the ratio of rates being approximately 0.02. This finding is consistent with the results obtained from population synthesis models. The formation of white dwarf mergers requires that the donor star is more massive than the white dwarf, and the mass of the donor is directly related to the rate of these events. The mass of the donor is determined by the rate of binary systems that survive common envelope evolution, and the resulting binary system has a mass for the donor of approximately 2.5 solar masses. The mass of the white dwarf is significantly affected by the rate of these events, and the resulting mass distribution of white dwarf mergers is not consistent with the single degenerate scenario. The formation of white dwarf mergers is also sensitive to the rate of common envelope ejection, and the resulting rate of these events is not significantly affected by the properties of the donor star. The formation of these events is also not significantly affected by the properties of the donor star. The formation of these events is also not significantly affected by the properties of the binary systems that produce them. The formation of these events is also not significantly affected by the properties of the binary systems that produce them.

In the context of online learning, we develop an online learning framework that can adapt to changing data distributions. We establish a theoretical foundation for this framework by analyzing the effects of chunk size and the learning rate. We demonstrate that by using smaller chunks of data and adjusting the learning rate accordingly, we can minimize the loss. Furthermore, we show that using larger chunks and setting a learning rate that grows linearly with the chunks can also yield an optimal result. These findings are supported by experiments on both artificial and real-world datasets, and the code used in the experiments is publicly available on GitHub.

The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in unprecedented health crises worldwide, necessitating a global response. The widespread vaccination efforts are hindered by challenges such as limited availability and varied accessibility. Digital Vaccine Passports have emerged as a solution to streamline vaccination processes and enhance transparency. This study explores the implementation of a robust vaccine passport system, focusing on its core components, their functionality, and the security protocols required. The paper also delves into the potential security and privacy threats, and presents an efficient solution to mitigate these issues using a Zero-Knowledge Proof technique. The proposed implementation demonstrates a high level of security, enabling users to manage their digital vaccination certificates. The solution adheres to the World Health Organization's privacy principles, and provides a secure, verifiable proof of vaccination through a Smart Contract on the Ethereum blockchain.

In the context of text datasets, topic classes often manifest as distinct groups within the space of sentence embeddings. This relationship enables the development of unsupervised topic modeling techniques that cluster sentences based on their corresponding embedding similarities. Although self-supervised sentence embeddings have made significant strides in capturing semantic meaning, they often lack the coherence and structural organization needed for unsupervised topic modeling. To address this limitation, we introduce a straightforward pre-training approach that enhances the quality of sentence embeddings through the incorporation of topic-level information. This pre-training method is rooted in the principle that topics should be consistent across different sentence embeddings and effectively groups sentences into coherent topic classes. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing the quality of sentence embeddings and generating meaningful topic models from unsupervised sentence embeddings.

We investigate the behavior of a non-interacting quantum particle within a spatially random environment that is characterized by a Gaussian distribution of potential energies. By employing the path-integral formulation, we derive the expression for the mean-squared displacement of a particle and subsequently determine the energy dependence of its diffusion coefficient. We find that this diffusion coefficient is directly proportional to energy, with a magnitude that is inversely related to the scale of the system's inherent uncertainty. We also examine the effects of different types of disorder distributions on the system's behavior, considering cases where the distribution of energy changes with the particle's energy.

The spin-lattice relaxation mechanism in nuclear magnetic resonance is a crucial method for determining the structure of molecules. It is also a key factor in understanding the spin relaxation of free electrons in the presence of a magnetic field. This study focuses on the spin relaxation of free electrons caused by interactions with nuclear spins in a specific type of semiconductor material, with the electrons' transverse spin undergoing relaxation. Our research reveals that the spin relaxation is influenced by a unique process involving the emission of a phonon by the nucleus, resulting in a time-dependent relaxation process distinct from previous findings. This new mechanism can be applied to other materials, such as solids with nuclear spins, providing a potential means to prolong the electron's transverse spin coherence time.

We investigate the behavior of a conformal field theory under periodic driving conditions, focusing on the return probability and energy density as key indicators. Our analysis reveals that below a certain crossover point, these metrics exhibit a time dependence consistent with the thermalization hypothesis. However, at and above this crossover time, the return probability and energy density deviate from their thermodynamic counterparts, with return probability scaling at late times as $t^{-\beta/3}$ and energy density scaling as $t^{-2}$ for a certain range of times. Our results demonstrate that the thermalization hypothesis is only valid in the low temperature and low time limit, with return probability and energy density deviating from thermal expectations at sufficiently large times.

This paper examines the relationship between compressed sensing and multimodal sensor fusion. Compressed sensing, which enables the recovery of missing data from redundant systems, is particularly relevant to sensor fusion, which combines multiple data sources to achieve a unified understanding. We investigate the connection between these two concepts through the lens of information fusion, specifically in Gaussian mixture models. Our findings show that in certain conditions, the most informative measurement for a particular data point can be represented as a weighted combination of its own attributes and the attributes of k-1 randomly selected data points, where k is significantly smaller than the total number of attributes. This result is more general and holds for a broader range of models, and we also derive a more precise upper limit for the number of measurements required to guarantee accurate recovery.

The Standard Model's prediction of the $C=\pm P$-violating phase has been highly accurate, making it difficult to use this method to detect new physics. We've found that the top quark's box diagram in a two Higgs doublet model shows significant sensitivity to the $C=P$ phase, as well as to the model's parameters. Analyzing the angular distributions of the $\gamma p \rightarrow t\bar{t}\pi^0$ reaction at the Thomas-Aquino-Willey laboratory could help set a more precise limit on the $C=P$ phase, as well as on the model's parameters, surpassing the current limits.

This study introduces a model-based control strategy for distributed systems with uncertain parameters, which balances performance, communication efficiency, and robustness against unknown disturbances. The controller adjusts its communication and computational processes in real-time to optimize performance under given constraints. The approach involves a hierarchical structure, where the system dynamically allocates control authority between local and distributed components to minimize communication overhead while maintaining desired performance levels. The controller's performance is evaluated through theoretical models and illustrated by numerical simulations of a network of sensors communicating with a central controller.

This letter examines the application of Bayesian filtering to track targets in scenarios utilizing multiple sensors. A key challenge arises from sensors operating within distinct domains, such as time and frequency, that must be synchronized. To address this issue, a novel solution is presented that leverages the Gibbs sampler to produce a labeled multi-Bernoulli birth distribution and enables the integration of sensed information from disparate domains. Additionally, a proposed filter utilizes a labeled multi-Bernoulli birth distribution to initiate track updates, incorporating the product of associated measurements in the likelihood function. Simulation results confirm the efficacy of the proposed filter, demonstrating its superiority over conventional approaches.

In this research, we investigate how interconnected properties affect the structure and organization of cultural and linguistic databases, with a specific focus on how certain characteristics are linked to one another. We've developed a method to measure these connections and applied it to a large dataset, revealing that features that are interrelated are clustered together. This enables the creation of new categories based on existing ones, allowing for more accurate predictions within these systems, which can then be tested and refined accordingly. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that these relationships are crucial for improving the accuracy of predictions, highlighting the importance of incorporating expert knowledge and additional features into the prediction process.

This paper conducts a comprehensive examination of advanced off-policy evaluation techniques. We provide a detailed mathematical analysis of existing off-policy evaluation methods, focusing on their statistical capabilities and the requirements necessary to achieve specific performance metrics and confidence levels. We then create a unified framework that encompasses multiple evaluation objectives commonly studied in the literature. Based on this framework, we identify key statistical properties for each objective and establish the necessary conditions for achieving them. We also identify the limitations of existing methods, proposing new techniques that address these constraints and demonstrate their efficacy in various evaluation objectives.

The traditional method of using mean and standard deviation to describe fermentation output variability is insufficient for accurately predicting outputs and fails to account for model uncertainties. This paper proposes a Bayesian approach to tackle these limitations. By treating a fermentation model as a probabilistic model, the Bayesian framework enables the quantification of uncertainty in predicted fermentation outputs and their variability. Through Bayesian inference, the proposed method can update model parameters and observations to reflect new data, making it suitable for applications such as optimizing feed compositions for protein yield maximization. The proposed method incorporates a Monte Carlo sampling technique, which can be integrated with existing optimization methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this Bayesian approach by applying it to a complex bioprocess model, showcasing its potential for efficient simulation and online data assimilation.

In the context of quantum physics, a specific type of effective action is used to describe particles that interact with a background field, such as a bosonic field. This action incorporates a term that represents the interaction between the particle and the field in a quadratic manner. When considering the movement of this particle in a specific way, its kinetic energy can be seen as equivalent to classical mass. To further investigate the properties of this particle, its effective action is modified to include a term that represents the interaction between the particle and the field in a linear manner. As a result, its effective mass changes in a specific way. Ultimately, the effects of this interaction on the particle's behavior are examined through a series of calculations that involve the transformation of its effective action into a form that represents its motion within a potential.

We've developed a novel approach to determine the electric flux decay rate, which is based on the assumption that it's caused by magnetic field diffusion. This method is applicable across various magnetic field configurations and scales. In the force-free electrodynamics context, we've discovered that the flux decay time is directly proportional to the 1/7 power of the magnetic field strength. Our findings are also relevant in the context of relativistic hydrodynamics, where we've established a correlation between the electric flux decay time and the 1/6 power of the system's energy density.

We investigate the minimal periodic decompositions of one-dimensional arrays of $n$-element patterns, which are characterized by the maximum number of segments under periodic constraints. This study involves the analysis of various pattern sets, including palindromes, binary sequences, primes, and Fibonacci numbers. We observe that the patterns with the lowest complexity validate Szabados's conjecture. Conversely, highly complex patterns require further investigation to confirm the validity of the conjecture. Additionally, our analysis of Fibonacci numbers reveals that they require an initial segment of a specific length, which increases as the Fibonacci number $F_n$ grows.
We establish that the Gromov-Hausdorff distance captures the essential characteristics of any given bounded metric space.

We address the asymptotic expansion of the resolvent $(\mathcal{L}_\varepsilon)-s)$ for the divergence form elliptic operator $\mathcal{L}_\varepsilon$ with a small parameter $\varepsilon$. Under a mild assumption on the coefficients, we derive an asymptotic expansion with a remainder term of higher order when compared to prior findings.

In this study, we examine the benefits of using explicit, standardized dialogue states in the development of dialogue systems. We argue that these states are a key component in the creation of robust dialogue applications. To support this claim, we present a controlled study comparing the effectiveness of controlled, standardized dialogue states against a more flexible approach. We discovered that incorporating explicit states not only simplifies the design process but also leads to better user engagement and more efficient task completion. Furthermore, we outline the trade-offs associated with the use of formal dialogue states and propose a set of guidelines for designers to consider when implementing them in their dialogue systems.

A new approach, Smt-Switch, is designed to improve the efficiency of applications that rely on Smt-Sat solvers by automatically switching between different solvers and incorporating user-defined constraints during search. This dynamic process is facilitated through a dynamic library interface that allows users to specify constraints and the desired search settings for each application. Smt-Switch is compatible with various libraries, including those for Z3, CVC4, and MathSAT, and its potential for enhancing performance has been demonstrated through multiple experiments with these libraries.

We have developed a new approach, known as Orthogonal Polynomial Projection Quantization (OPPQ), to numerically find the eigenstates of the Schrödinger equation. This method utilizes a specific type of projection that incorporates orthogonal polynomials, resulting in a more efficient and accurate calculation. When applied to nearly exact solutions, the OPPQ method demonstrates exceptional stability and rapid convergence. However, the method's performance is significantly impacted when calculating quasi-exactly solvable states, producing a unique distribution of eigenvalues. Our research also explores the practical applications of OPPQ in the context of real-world systems, such as semiconductor nanostructures, and compares its results to those obtained using the Finite Element Method (FEM).

A novel approach to enhance the efficiency of CNNs involves a two-stage training process. Initially, a "digital twin" CNN is trained with a focus on increasing the input resolution to twice its original size. Next, the trained model is used to generate a new set of images with the elevated resolution, followed by the retraining of the original CNN using these synthesized images. This iterative process is repeated until it reaches a predetermined stopping point. Through this process, the original CNN achieves improved performance on various tasks while maintaining its original efficiency, as demonstrated in our experiments with image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks.

The rotation of a binary star's secondary component can be determined by analyzing the patterns of brightness on its surface. However, if the secondary star is a fast rotator, the effects of rotation are masked by its surface activity, making it difficult to determine its rotation rate. Researchers have proposed a method to determine the rotation rate of active stars based on the patterns of brightness on their surface, without making assumptions about how active they are. This method uses data from the GALEN satellite and has been applied to 12 binary star systems, 7 of which have been studied for the first time. The results show that the rotation rates of these stars can be determined with an accuracy of 10-20%. This method has been compared to other methods of determining rotation rates and has been found to be the most accurate.

We have investigated the existence and stability of long-range charged particle clouds that orbit around black holes in a specific theoretical framework known as Einstein-Vlasov theory, where black holes are described by the Schwarzschild solution. To this end, we have developed a numerical method to find the particles' equilibrium states and their associated stability. Our study has shown that certain types of potential allow for the existence of such particle clouds, and we have identified the conditions under which they are stable or unstable. Our results also indicate that when these particle clouds do become unstable, they collapse into a black hole, and we have determined the masses of these new black holes.

We investigate the potential of future electron neutrino and antineutrino experiments to detect active-sterile neutrino oscillations, specifically under the assumption of a single sterile state. The analysis takes into account the impact of a single parameter, the mass splitting between the active and sterile neutrinos, and the magnitudes of the associated neutrino mixing amplitudes. The results show that these experiments can establish constraints on the parameter space governing active-sterile neutrino interactions, and that they may be comparable to those set by existing experiments on the active-sterile neutrino mixing amplitudes.

We introduce a new image denoising technique that utilizes a combination of a conditional variational flow (CVF) and a denoising diffusion model (DDM). The CVF module is trained to separate clean images from noisy data using a probabilistic approach, focusing on areas with the highest noise levels. The DDM is responsible for learning the distribution of the remaining noisy data. By integrating these two components, we achieve a model that can effectively capture the complex noise structure. Through rigorous evaluation on both artificial and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over current state-of-the-art image denoising techniques.

We introduce a novel approach to determining the number of samples required for recovering sparse signals from measurements in the presence of noise, utilizing the knowledge of the maximum absolute value of the signal's coefficients as a parameter. This method is applied to the problem of recovering a k-sparse signal from noisy measurements of its inner products with randomly chosen vectors, and yields a bound on the number of samples needed that tightens as the signal's absolute coefficients increase. Specifically, for k-sparse signals with k equal to a fixed constant, we demonstrate that the required number of samples is bounded from above and below by a function that scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{k}\log(1/\epsilon))$. This result is achieved by utilizing the fact that a k-sparse signal can be represented as the difference between two signals, each with a limited number of non-zero coefficients, and by employing a combinatorial argument to count the possible differences between two sets of non-zero coefficients.

Developing programs with strong guarantees using higher-order contracts is complicated, 
particularly in union and intersection types which increase complexity. To address this issue, 
we've created a system that simplifies contract writing for such types by using a new abstraction 
that replaces complex type combinations with a more manageable concept we call "contractors". 
These contractors encapsulate the details of complex type patterns, significantly reducing the 
difficulty of working with higher-order contracts.

Recent breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have led to the development of novel
architectures, such as the World-Modeler, which enables the learning of complex
tasks like video game behaviors. Building on this, we've created a new framework
that integrates intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards. Our findings indicate
that this dual approach significantly accelerates the training process. Furthermore, we've analyzed the policy learning dynamics and discovered that a
policy's representation can evolve in two distinct manners, either by refining
task-specific details or discovering new, abstract strategies.

We investigate the oscillatory behavior of a particle in an anharmonic potential under the influence of dissipative forces, using a specific setup to analyze its motion within a particular potential. By examining the properties of its trajectory, we derive the parameters that define its frequency of oscillation, which enables us to compare classical and quantum-mechanical predictions. Our analysis reveals discrepancies between these frameworks when the potential is highly anharmonic, particularly for high-frequency modes, while for lower frequencies, the agreement is found to be satisfactory.

We examine the two-point functions for the metric and matter in a simplified, yet dynamic, model of string theory with a specific type of background. These functions represent the result of decoupling string theory's multiple modes, and their behavior is derived from summing over various string networks that satisfy specific conditions. Notably, the functions' behavior is influenced by the relative contributions of different string topologies, and their behavior is often controlled by specific mathematical functions. These functions' behavior is further affected by the relative importance of different string topologies, and they can exhibit unusual behavior such as sudden changes in their rates of growth or decay.

We investigated rule violations on Twitter to understand behavior changes in suspended users. Analyzing 82 million tweets over two years, we found that suspended users violated rules more frequently than others, particularly in new guidelines introduced in 2017. This trend persisted even after removal of known automated accounts, indicating that suspended users' violation rates were driven by controlled manual tweeting, not automated software. This study provides a comprehensive view of rule violations on Twitter, offering insights into the intricacies of its content moderation system.

The European X-band project is a collaborative effort between CERN and Fermilab aimed at developing a high-energy, compact S-band linac that utilizes advanced 4.5 GeV, 10 kW RF technology. This technology has the potential to significantly impact the design of future accelerators and the corresponding experiments, particularly with regards to electron-hadron and hadron-hadron collisions. By utilizing the same RF power and framework as the Fermilab Front-End Test Facility, the European X-band project will facilitate the development of complex linac design components and ultimately evaluate the linac in a realistic environment, utilizing the same infrastructure for a wide range of tests.

Deep learning networks have shown resilience in dealing with noisy labels, but they often rely on assumptions that real-world data doesn't meet. This study investigates how using multiple models in an ensemble to address uncertain labels affects performance, particularly when dealing with difficult-to-separate classes. We examine both the impact of ensembles on accurate versus incorrect classifications and their overall effectiveness in learning, with a specific focus on networks that struggle with separation. Our analysis, based on simple mathematical models, shows that learning from uncertain labels can actually be more effective than achieving perfect separation, and that this advantage can be enhanced through ensembles of multiple models.

This study examines the resource allocation problem in V2X communications, focusing on ensuring the safety of vulnerable road users. A novel approach is presented, where available resources are distributed among vehicles based on their respective weights, which are determined by their vulnerability levels. A resource allocation mechanism and associated algorithm are proposed to effectively assign these weights. This method prioritizes resources for vehicles in high-risk situations, while also optimizing overall network efficiency. Simulation results demonstrate the performance enhancements offered by this approach over conventional methods.

The rapid advancement in Artificial Intelligence technologies has given rise to significant concerns regarding their impact on society's overall transparency and fairness. In this context, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art in AI explainability and fairness. A thorough review of existing approaches in these two interconnected areas will serve as the foundation for identifying both shared challenges and opportunities for improvement. Furthermore, we will outline potential solutions to facilitate the integration of explainability and fairness by leveraging established methods, and by providing guidance on practical applications.

This research examines the relationship between feature toggles and the efficiency of managing software branches. Based on data from 9 Java projects that utilize feature toggles, our analysis reveals that the use of feature toggles leads to a notable decrease in the integration of branches, albeit without a significant impact on the overall codebase modification rate. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the quality of branch merges remains unaffected by feature toggle adoption. Notably, our study indicates that high-quality feature toggles tend to have a greater impact on improving integration efficiency compared to those that are poorly maintained. The results of our study are based on a comprehensive dataset of 24.6 million commits and 1.2 billion modified lines of code across 1.1 billion branch merges.

The conservation of enstrophy is examined within the context of Lagrangian fluid dynamics, revealing an apparent contradiction between Euler's equation and the conservation law. Upon closer inspection, it becomes clear that the discrepancy arises due to a neglect of the effects of molecular diffusion. To reconcile the discrepancy, two methods can be employed: the inclusion of a random perturbation to account for molecular diffusion or the application of a Smoluchowski equation to model the breakup of turbulent eddies. Both approaches yield a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation that conserves enstrophy locally, thus resolving the discrepancy.

We propose "Maximum Attention", a straightforward yet effective method to visually examine how a trained network utilizes attention mechanisms. It involves computing the attention maps by taking the gradient of the output score with respect to each attention patch, thereby illustrating the most critical areas for feature extraction. We demonstrate the applicability and efficiency of this approach through various experiments on tasks such as image classification, object localization, and question answering, where we successfully identify important regions, even when other methods fail to do so.

We've developed a novel method for calculating loop effects involving massive spin-2 fields at the one-loop level. This approach is adaptable to a broad range of theories featuring massive spin-2 fields as new physical entities. We've applied this method to investigate the one-loop mass corrections for the graviton in a model where a massive spin-2 field is coupled with a massless spin-1 graviton field. This research has implications for theories beyond the Standard Model that include massive spin-2 fields, such as those involving massive gravity, spontaneous symmetry breaking, and theories with extra dimensions.

Research on the peace and war processes often relies on empirical data, but we aim to simulate a complex polity's decision-making processes on war and peace, incorporating the effects of political biases. A polity is modeled as an interconnected network of agents, each with individual preferences and the capacity to influence the decisions of surrounding agents, influenced by their interconnected relationships. We demonstrate that a polity's strategic decisions on war and peace are influenced by inherent political biases, with biases in decision-making processes leading to distorted expectations about war and peace outcomes. Notably, a polity's bias can skew its expectations in multiple ways, making war or peace negotiations more appealing under certain circumstances.

Our research involved using MEG to examine how the brain processes arguments linked to roles within sentences. A novel approach was employed to isolate and compare neural activities for arguments of different thematic roles within the same sentence. Our study found that instantiations of words with the same part-of-speech and grammatical case showed significant overlap when combined, whereas words with different thematic roles activations did not overlap significantly. This overlap suggests that when words instantiating the same role are present in a sentence, the brain treats them similarly, and this may have implications for how the brain processes and integrates linguistic elements.

The detection of massive objects such as black holes or neutron stars by gravitational wave interferometers relies heavily on the identification of neutrinos that originate from these sources. Researchers have developed a new method to pinpoint the location of such triggers using neutrinos, which does not require knowledge of the neutrino's direction of emission. The new method utilizes a neural network trained on a large dataset of mock neutrino sky maps to determine the location of the neutrino in three-dimensional space. The findings indicate that the accuracy of the neural network's predictions is directly related to the accuracy of the neutrino's time and energy measurements. When these measurements are precise enough to resolve the angular size of a few degrees, the neural network's predictions of the neutrino's location match the actual location to within a few hundred meters. The method's effectiveness in localizing the neutrino in three-dimensional space is particularly important for the detection of massive objects by gravitational wave and neutrino detectors.

The spatial Power Spectral Density (PSD) of the Proba3 Colleger Chabre's Point Spread Function (PSF) measurements were analyzed in relation to the Proba3 mission's primary mirror seeing and the Proba3's coronagraph's tip-tenion wavefront error. The spatial PSD was found to be directly proportional to the primary mirror seeing squared and inversely proportional to the square root of the coronagraph's wavefront error. The study also found a linear relationship between the primary mirror seeing and the total PSD, with the PSD being more sensitive to the primary mirror seeing than to the coronagraph's wavefront error.

The accuracy of phonon dispersion simulations significantly depends on the chosen electronic structure method. To assess this, we utilized the r2SCAN density functional to calculate and compare the phonon dispersion curves of Al, Tl, Na, and Ti with experimental data. The r2SCAN results showed improved agreement with experiments at zero temperature compared to the PBE functional, particularly for Ti, yet showed a contradictory trend with increasing temperature. As a result, we recommend utilizing the r2SCAN functional at room temperature for phonon simulations but suggest avoiding its use in elevated temperature scenarios due to inaccuracies.

This study offers a universal method to determine coverability sets for very-WSTS (well-structured transition systems) in a finite amount of time, as long as the size of the set is also finite. Additionally, it presents an algorithm for computing the coverability set of a system within a finite time, given its initial state. The findings can be applied to a broad range of infinite systems, including Petri nets and various systems related to program analysis, while also providing a finite-time algorithm for computing the highest semidefinite coverability sets of certain systems.

The long-term monitoring of active galactic nuclei using the XMM-Newton observatory has been a key project, with over 2000 sources monitored to date. Our research involves analyzing variability patterns in a subset of these sources, with observations spanning more than 2.5 million XMM-Newton exposures. This study is challenging due to the varying quality of data and the long time frames of the observations. To address these complexities, we employed a novel approach that accounts for data and time variability before selecting the most suitable datasets for analysis. Our results show that the majority of the sources in our sample exhibit significant variability, with a small percentage displaying complex light curves. We further investigated the light curves of the sources by dividing them into sub-samples based on their characteristics, such as the soft and hard energy bands. Our findings reveal that soft and hard energy bands exhibit similar variability patterns, with a notable exception in a few sources. We also observed that soft and hard energy bands display similar variability amplitudes, with a few exceptions, such as the sources displaying a soft lag.

Quantum Darwinism offers a resolution to the quantum origin mystery by explaining
how objective reality forms through the interaction of a system with its surroundings,
resulting in the emergence of distinct objective properties. This theory reveals that
the information needed to define an object's state is dispersed among many aspects
of the environment, making it difficult to identify in a single location. Research
on quantum Darwinism has primarily focused on systems at thermal equilibrium. This
study expands on this concept by examining systems out of equilibrium, which are
described by non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. The researchers demonstrate that a system's
surrounding environment can provide clues to its non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, making
it possible to measure this parameter through a process that does not require
projective measurements.

This research introduces an innovative method for approximating the reachable set of discrete-time dynamical systems consisting of multiple interconnected linear state-space systems. By leveraging the concepts of convex bodies and ellipsoids, the authors demonstrate how the limits of these systems can be estimated and represented graphically through the application of minimal convex polytopes, which are derived from the analysis of the individual system limits. By utilizing these approximations, the authors develop efficient algorithms for calculating the reachable set and solving related optimization problems, such as reachability and feasibility, which are then demonstrated through numerical examples.

The SAINT model, a self-attention based neural network, has been shown to deliver superior performance on tabular data problems through its ability to effectively model high-dimensional data. This study further explores the model's capabilities, establishing new benchmarks in the field of tabular data through the model's performance on various datasets. Furthermore, a new method for training SAINT has been developed, which significantly improves the model's sample efficiency and allows for the training of larger models. As a result, the model's performance on several benchmarks has been enhanced, with the model's improved accuracy and broader applicability to the field of tabular data.

The effectiveness of transfer learning in improving performance on downstream tasks using pre-trained models is well-established, but the underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood. This study investigates how the similarity between the models were trained on (source) and the models are being adapted for (target) affects the performance gain from transfer learning. We examine this in the context of natural language processing, where we compare model performance on two datasets with varying levels of similarity. Our analysis suggests that transfer learning benefits are most significant when applied to similar tasks with similar data, and we propose a new metric to quantify this similarity.

In quantum chromodynamics, the breaking of chiral symmetry is observed in certain regions of the interaction kernel, leading to the formation of quark condensates. This breaking results in a distinction between left and right particles, influencing the behavior of interacting particles in these areas. This paper examines how the properties of the interaction kernel affect the size of chiral symmetry breaking regions and the structure of the condensates within them.

The search focuses on vector-like quarks that decay into dark matter particles and a specific set of particles, and looks for signs of this decay in the form of missing transverse momentum and a specific set of particles. The study uses a dataset of around 36.1 and 46.3 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions. The study's results are presented in the form of a limit on the interaction between the vector-like quark and the dark matter particles, and this interaction is found to be consistent with the Standard Model. Identifying the location of a software concept is a crucial task that is often hindered by the lack of relevant information in crowdsourced platforms. Typically, concept location tools rely solely on individual text inputs without considering the collective knowledge of the community. To address this limitation, researchers have developed an innovative approach that integrates community data to pinpoint software concepts. By leveraging the community-driven aspect, this method successfully localizes software components within large-scale systems, such as specific Java classes within Eclipse.

This study introduces a block-diagonal preconditioner to enhance the numerical solution of the two-dimensional singular two-point boundary value problem, specifically for ODE systems. Notably, the proposed preconditioner exhibits a block-diagonal structure, and its efficacy is demonstrated through various numerical examples that show its performance under Krylov subspace methods.

In the field of natural language processing, summarizing dialogues without explicit guidance is a complex challenge. To tackle this issue, researchers have been utilizing various discourse relation extraction techniques to inform the generation of abstract summaries. This paper introduces a new method that automatically extracts discourse relations without relying on specific rules or external resources, and leverages these relations to create informative summaries. The proposed approach relies on a neural network that combines dialogue context and extracted relations to produce a concise summary. The experiments conducted on two publicly available datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the new method, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches for abstract dialogue summarization.

This study introduces a cutting-edge approach that leverages deep learning to efficiently compute the Doppler broadening of cross-sections for high-energy applications. The proposed method is thoroughly tested using the fast neutron activation of argon-38 at the high-energy proton accelerator of the National Superconducting Cyclotron Laboratory, where the activation cross-sections are calculated using the TALYS nuclear reaction code and analyzed using the Doppler-Broaden cross-sections. The performance of the approach is evaluated and verified by comparing the results from two different neural networks, demonstrating the feasibility of this novel method for high-energy neutron activation analysis.

This study aims to introduce a new concept of $(n+1)$-pre-Lie algebras by building upon the existing knowledge of $n$-pre-Lie algebras. It further explores the underlying generalized trace maps for $(n+1)$-pre-Live algebras and establishes a connection to multi-Trace type operators. Additionally, this paper proposes the notion of $(n+1)$-pre-Lie bialgebras as a combination of traditional $n$-pre-Lie algebras and co-gebra structures.

A novel scheme is introduced to address the challenge of providing quality assurance for real-time users in shared wireless networks, contrasting with conventional methods that prioritize them or neglect the varying requirements of different users. The proposed approach prioritizes real-time and shared users in consecutive time slots, ensuring fair resource allocation and throughput for all users. Mathematical analysis confirms that this scheme yields higher overall system throughput and shared users' throughput compared to prioritizing real-time users alone. Additionally, it ensures real-time users receive a higher share of the total available throughput than the 50% threshold under the total packet dropping probability of 0.01. Simulation results demonstrate that this scheme outperforms existing approaches, such as the Round Robin policy and the total packet dropping probability of 0.01 under the total users' throughput compared to prioritizing real-time users alone.
